title: Throughput quench probe: two‑phase ramp / quick‑drop experiments
content:
Purpose:
Quick informal writeup of a set of 'quench' experiments I ran to understand latency tail behaviour when a high QPS ramp is abruptly quenched to a low steady QPS (simulates flash-sale style traffic that then drops). Goal is to capture observable prime/decay dynamics, KV cache hit interplay, and where warmup/eviction penalties show up in p95/p99.

Run summary (high level):
- Model: rw-v2-3B-quant (FP16-ish quant profile) mounted as variant v2025-01-q1
- Serving pool: dedicated smallpool-A (4xA10G, 32GB per GPU), 8 worker replicas, shared KV cache across workers via local LRU (8M entries)
- Sequence length: typical 128 tokens request, median prompt 72 tokens
- Client pattern: two-phase per trial:
    1) RAMP: linear from 5 qps -> 350 qps over 60s (aggressive ramp)
    2) QUENCH: sudden drop to 10 qps sustained for 300s
- Duration per trial: 6m (including settling windows)
- Trials: 8 full trials over 2 hours (varied cooling threshold and warm-cache percentage)

Why this pattern:
- Common for e‑commerce or notification blasts where a surge finishes quickly then a long tail of low traffic remains. We suspect evictions + background GC + kernel coldstart produce two separate latency components: an immediate transient (50–120s) and a longer tail (200–600s) as caches re-equilibrate.

Instrumentation collected:
- Per-request: client-side timestamp, server enqueue, start_exec, end_exec, kv_hit(bool), worker_id, kernel-version tag
- Periodic: gpu_util, mem_used, swap_pressure, OS page-in/out counters, per-worker KV cache size
- Aggregates: p50/p90/p95/p99, QPS, concurrency, kv_hit_rate over 5s windows

Key observations (numbers are medians/aggregates across trials):
- During ramp peak (300–350 qps):
    - p50 ~ 55 ms, p95 ~ 140 ms, p99 ~ 310 ms
    - KV overall hit-rate falls ~ 0.72 -> 0.61 when ramp crosses 200 qps (eviction pressure)
    - GPU util steady ~ 92–96% (saturated path)
- Immediately after quench (first 30s):
    - p50 drops quickly to 48 ms, but p95/p99 spike: p95 ~ 220 ms, p99 ~ 720 ms (worst trials up to 1.1s)
    - Concurrently observed a surge of page-in activity on two workers (worker 3 & 6) and small GC cycles triggered (Python worker-level heap compaction)
- Medium term (30–180s after quench):
    - p95 decays slowly from 220 -> 120 ms; p99 from 720 -> 260 ms
    - KV hit-rate recovers gradually back to ~0.70 over ~150–200s
    - Observed periodic microspikes (200–400ms) on a single worker every ~45s — correlated with disk I/O flush on that worker (log rotation triggered at 00:00 UTC mistakenly during a long run)
- Long tail (>180s):
    - Metrics stabilize: p50 ~ 46 ms, p95 ~ 100 ms, p99 ~ 160 ms
    - Background eviction/gc quiets; util ~ 12–20% at 10 qps

Notable failure modes / anomalies:
- One trial exhibited persistent p99 ~ 500ms for >8 minutes after quench. Root cause: worker 6 had a transient NVME latency spike (thermal throttle) causing OS-level page-in stalls; correlated with hotter-than-usual storage temps reported by infra logs.
- Another trial had elevated p95 due to a kernel variant fallback: on worker 1 the serving runtime switched to safer matmul kernel (fallback) for 90s when a micro assert hit early in the ramp — increased latency but avoided errors. The fallback was controlled by 'kernel-safety' patch that recently landed (PR #2145).

Quick ASCII timeline (one representative trial, averaged windows):
- 0–60s: ramp -> qps climbs 5 -> 350; p99 climbs steadily (100ms -> 300ms)
- 60s (quench): qps jumps to 10; p50 drops, p99 spikes then decays

Time (s) | QPS  | p50(ms) | p95(ms) | p99(ms) | kv_hit
0        | 5    | 48      | 110     | 190     | 0.74
30       | 120  | 52      | 130     | 240     | 0.69
60       | 350  | 55      | 140     | 310     | 0.61
90       | 10   | 50      | 220     | 720     | 0.56
240      | 10   | 47      | 120     | 260     | 0.67
420      | 10   | 46      | 100     | 160     | 0.70

Hints / hypotheses:
- Quench spike likely from two sources: (1) sudden drop causes concurrency to collapse and a fraction of in-flight requests face cache misses and kernel reinitialization overheads, (2) OS-level paging/IO contention uncovered under high memory churn during ramp.
- The KV cache policy (LRU global across workers) seems to produce suboptimal steady-state when quench moves working set quickly — consider sticky per-worker segments + fast re-warm path.
- Kernel fallback events amplify spikes; we should ensure metrics flag fallback occurrences as high-severity alerts (current alerting only logs them).

Next steps / actionable items:
- Repeat with: (A) per-worker pinned KV segments (50/50 split) vs global LRU; (B) reduced logging at high throughput to avoid NVME pressure; (C) run with kernel-safety toggled off for comparison to measure pure latency impact (controlled run).
- Add histograms + waterfall traces for the first 120s after quench so we can separate queuing vs exec vs kv-miss costs.
- Ask infra to check NVME thermal profile on pool-A (ticket created INF-4917).
- Create a lightweight SLO checkpoint: emit a "quench_event" marker to traces and a per-replica kv_miss_breakdown; useful for automated regression detection.

Notes to self:
- Write a short PRD note for sticky-cache experiment and link to community notes.
- This pattern reproduces in staged Dedicated pools and in private VPC infra; might be customer-visible for bursty ecommerce clients.

Appendix: quick run checklist used for each trial:
- Clear KV cache snapshot (start-of-trial marker)
- Restart workers (graceful) -> ensure kernel-variant consistent
- Sync clocks (ntp) and start client driver (replay tool v0.9b)
- Collect logs: /var/log/serving/*.log and /proc/diskstats every 5s

End.
